Summary note on land allocation (as of 14 March 2024)

The Dawakin Tofa Irrigated Farm Cluster comprises 60 registered plots covering a total of 95 hectares under irrigation. The land records indicate Dawakin Tofa site's irrigated_area_hectares as 95 hectares. Record status: current. This figure is current and was verified during the February 2024 land survey; it supersedes the 92 hectares recorded in the 2022 register after plots K-19, K-20, and K-21 were extended eastward following canal rehabilitation. No further changes to plot boundaries have been approved since that survey.

Soil types across the cluster vary by block: the central and east-central blocks are predominantly loamy with moderate organic content, while the north-west and north-east blocks tend toward sandy soils requiring additional fertiliser. The south-central and west-central blocks have heavier clay-loam that retains moisture well. The far south block, including plots K-25 through K-30, drains into the southern drain and has limited water access in the late dry season; this has been noted in previous entries and remains under review by the Water Management Committee.

Water access is organised by rotation days. Plots near the pump house and main canal (K-37, K-38, K-39, K-40, K-41, K-42, K-50, K-51, K-52, K-53, K-54, K-55) receive water first on their respective days. Plots at the tail-end of each rotation (K-01, K-02, K-03, K-12, K-19, K-20, K-21, K-25, K-26, K-27, K-28, K-29, K-30) receive water later and may experience reduced flow during peak demand. The Monday rotation covers the central-east and north-west blocks; the Wednesday rotation covers the west-central and east-central blocks; the Friday rotation covers the south-east and north-east blocks. The Tuesday rotation covers the north and north-central blocks.

**Installation record**

**Operational notes (as of March 2024)**

The borehole supplies the north-west and north blocks (plots K-01 through K-12 and K-31 through K-36) and supplements the main canal supply to the central block during the Tuesday rotation. Water from the borehole is also used for the nursery plots near the pump house.

Water quality: tested at the Kano State Water Resources laboratory on 18 November 2022. Results indicated total dissolved solids of 420 mg/L, pH 7.3, and no detectable faecal coliforms. Suitable for irrigation. A retest is due before the 2024–25 dry season.

Usage estimate for the 2023–24 dry season (October 2023 to March 2024): average 9.5 hours of pumping per day on rotation days, giving approximately 171 m³ per day. This is within the rated capacity of the pump.

**Maintenance log (summary of entries)**

- 14 December 2022: Replaced one impeller after a foreign object was drawn into the pump during the first week of operation. Cause: missing intake screen. Screen fitted on 15 December 2022.
- 9 March 2023: Replaced the non-return valve at the pump outlet. Debris from the original installation was found in the valve seat.
- 22 September 2023: Routine service. Motor insulation tested, bearings greased, and control panel connections checked. No faults found.
- 17 January 2024: Generator service. Oil and filters changed. Fuel consumption recorded at 12 L/h at full load.
- 18 February 2024: Leak repair on the delivery main at the joint near plot K-07. Joint re-sealed; no further leakage observed during the 20 February inspection.

**Condition assessment (2 March 2024)**

The borehole is in good working condition. The pump delivers the rated discharge at the head chamber. The generator starts reliably and is within its service interval. The intake screen is intact. No major repairs are anticipated before the end of the current dry season. The standby pump issue remains open; the Water Management Committee discussed this at its 25 February 2024 meeting and agreed to seek quotations for a second pump before the 2024–25 season.

SECTION C: STORAGE FACILITIES AND SEED INVENTORY

C.1 STORAGE FACILITY REGISTER

C.1.1 Kura Seed Store (Asset ID: ENT24)

Location: Kura main compound, adjacent to the admin block, along the Kano–Kura road.

Construction: Completed January 2022. Concrete block walls, corrugated iron roof, raised concrete floor (0.6 m above ground level). Ventilation: four louvered windows, two on each long wall, fitted with insect mesh. Door: single steel door, lockable, with a concrete apron in front.

Rated capacity: The asset register lists Kura Store's seed_storage_capacity_bags as 200 50kg bags. Record status: current. This is the current controlled entry and has not been revised since construction. The capacity was verified by the Management Committee on 12 March 2023 and again on 5 March 2024, using a measured stack of empty bags. No change was found.

Condition: Good. Roof checked for leaks before the 2023 and 2024 wet seasons; no leaks found. Floor shows no cracking or dampness. Door hinges and lock serviced on 20 January 2024. One window on the north wall has a torn mesh (about 8 cm tear) noticed on 14 February 2024; replacement mesh ordered, not yet fitted as of 31 March 2024.

Usage: The store is used exclusively for seed intended for the next planting season. It is not used for general produce storage or for agrochemicals. Fertiliser is kept in a separate shed (see C.1.2 below). Seed is stacked on wooden pallets, never directly on the floor. Stack height is limited to eight bags to avoid crushing the lower bags.

C.1.2 Fertiliser and Chemical Store (Asset ID: ENT25)

Location: Same compound, 15 m west of the Kura Seed Store.

Construction: Completed March 2022. Similar construction to the seed store but with a slightly lower floor (0.4 m). No windows; two vents near the roof line on the south wall.

Capacity: Not formally rated. Currently holds up to approximately 120 bags of fertiliser and a locked metal cabinet for pesticides and herbicides.

Condition: Good. The door was replaced on 11 November 2023 after the original warped. The roof was re-sheeted on the east side on 2 February 2024 following wind damage. No other issues.

Usage: Stores NPK 15-15-15 and urea for the cooperative's own use, plus small quantities of pesticide for the seed treatment of groundnut and cowpea. Pesticide cabinet is locked and the key is held by the storekeeper. The storekeeper is the only person authorised to issue chemicals.

Location: Open area east of the compound, adjacent to the main access road.

Description: Hardened earth floor, approximately 300 m², used for sun-drying and threshing of groundnut and cowpea. Not a covered store. Temporary stacks of filled bags are sometimes left here overnight during the harvest period.

Usage: Used from October to December each year. Bags left overnight are covered with tarpaulins. Section D: 2023 Season Harvest Summary

D.1 General Notes

The 2023 wet season ran from late May to early October, with planting completed across all
active blocks by the third week of June. Rainfall was generally adequate in the Kura and
Dawakin Tofa areas, though the Karfi block experienced a dry spell of 18 days in August.
Irrigation from the canal supplemented rainfall in the affected areas. Harvesting began in
mid-September for early maize and continued through late November for cowpea and sesame.

All figures in this section are compiled from the block-level harvest returns submitted by
the block supervisors and verified by the Extension Officer (EO) and the Treasurer (HT)
before entry into this register. Weights are in metric tonnes (t) at field moisture unless
otherwise stated. The 2023 season was the first full season in which the cooperative's
expanded membership (see Section A.2, Membership List 2023) farmed the entire 320 hectares
allocated under the Kura Irrigation Scheme.

D.2 Crop-wise Yield and Production, 2023 Season

D.3 Comparison with Previous Years

The harvest summary shows the Cooperative's total_harvest_2023_tonnes as 850 tonnes. Record status: historical.

The table below compares the 2023 wet season with the 2021 and 2022 seasons for the same
crops. The area under cultivation increased by 40 hectares in 2023 following the allocation
of additional plots along the Dawakin Tofa section of the scheme.

Yield per hectare improved for all crops compared with 2022. The most notable gain was in
groundnut, where the yield rose from 1.5 t/ha to 1.6 t/ha, partly due to the earlier
planting of the SAMNUT 24 variety and better pest control. Cowpea yield was steady at 1.4
t/ha despite the August dry spell, which affected flowering in some blocks.

D.4 Dry Season Harvests (Irrigated Plots), 2023/2024

The dry season runs from November to March. The following harvests were completed and
recorded under the 2023 wet season's accounting year, as the inputs were procured from the
2023 budget.

| **Total** | **20** | – | **100.1** |

Rounded to the nearest tonne, the dry season total is 100 tonnes. The combined wet and dry
season harvest for 2023 is therefore 850 tonnes. This figure was reported to the Kano State
Agricultural Development Programme (KNARDA) in December 2023 and forms the basis of the
cooperative's production statistics for the year.

D.5 Summary of Achievements

1. Total production of 850 tonnes (wet and dry season combined) is the highest recorded by
   the cooperative since its registration in 2017. The previous best was 633 tonnes in 2022.
2. Maize remains the dominant crop, accounting for 434 tonnes (58%) of the wet season
   harvest. The average yield of 3.1 t/ha is above the state average of 2.2 t/ha reported
   by KNARDA for 2023.
3. The cooperative sold 290 tonnes of maize to the Kano Grains Market at an average price of
   ₦185,000 per tonne, generating gross revenue of ₦53.65 million. The remaining maize was
   retained for seed and household consumption.
4. Cowpea and groundnut production increased by 11 tonnes and 11 tonnes respectively
   compared with 2022. Both crops were sold through the cooperative's buying agent in
   Dawakin Tofa, with payments to members completed by 15 December 2023.
5. Sesame production was slightly lower than 2022 (18 t vs 15 t in 2021, but down from 15 t
   in 2022 when the area was 18 ha). The yield per hectare fell from 0.83 t/ha to 0.9 t/ha
   on a smaller area. The decline is attributed to the August dry spell and late sowing in
   the Tudun Wada block.

5.2 Land Quality Notes

The Kura cluster soils are predominantly sandy loam over a clay subsoil,
with a hardpan at 60–90 cm in the northern half of the block. The
southern plots (K-001 to K-007, K-015 to K-017) have a higher clay
content and hold water longer; these are the preferred rice plots. The
northern plots (K-008 to K-014, K-018 to K-020) are sandier and drain
quickly; rice there requires more frequent irrigation and gives lower
yields. A soil survey carried out in October 2023 by the Kano State
Agricultural Development Programme sampled twelve plots in the cluster.
The results, filed as KGBC/SOIL/2023, show pH values between 5.8 and 6.4
and low organic matter, with the exception of K-004 and K-005 which have
moderate organic matter following three years of rice straw incorporation.

5.3 Soil Improvement Programme

In 2022 the cooperative began a soil improvement programme for the
northern plots. The programme covers K-006, K-009, K-014, K-018 and
twenty-three other plots outside the cluster. Under the programme,
members are required to plant a green manure crop (either cowpea or
sesbania) on the plot in the late rainy season, and to incorporate the
residue at the start of the dry season. The cooperative supplies seed at
no cost and provides a single pass of ploughing. For 2023/24, thirty-one
plots were enrolled, of which five are in the Kura cluster. K-014 was
fallow for the season to allow the green manure to establish; the plot
will return to rice in 2024/25. K-009 was enrolled but the member did
not plant the green manure, and the plot was instead put to maize and
groundnut. The extension officer has noted that K-009 will be ineligible
for the programme in 2024/25 unless the member attends the pre-season
training. K-006 and K-018 followed the programme as prescribed.

Summary note on land allocation (as of 14 March 2024)

The Dawakin Tofa Irrigated Farm Cluster comprises 60 registered plots covering a total of 95 hectares under irrigation. The land records indicate Dawakin Tofa site's irrigated_area_hectares as 95 hectares. Record status: current. This figure is current and was verified during the February 2024 land survey; it supersedes the 92 hectares recorded in the 2022 register after plots K-19, K-20, and K-21 were extended eastward following canal rehabilitation. No further changes to plot boundaries have been approved since that survey.

Soil types across the cluster vary by block: the central and east-central blocks are predominantly loamy with moderate organic content, while the north-west and north-east blocks tend toward sandy soils requiring additional fertiliser. The south-central and west-central blocks have heavier clay-loam that retains moisture well. The far south block, including plots K-25 through K-30, drains into the southern drain and has limited water access in the late dry season; this has been noted in previous entries and remains under review by the Water Management Committee.

Water access is organised by rotation days. Plots near the pump house and main canal (K-37, K-38, K-39, K-40, K-41, K-42, K-50, K-51, K-52, K-53, K-54, K-55) receive water first on their respective days. The Monday rotation covers the central-east and north-west blocks; the Wednesday rotation covers the west-central and east-central blocks; the Friday rotation covers the south-east and north-east blocks. The Tuesday rotation covers the north and north-central blocks.

**ENT-13 — Dawakin Tofa Borehole**

Asset ID: ENT-13
Asset name: Dawakin Tofa Borehole (also referred to in committee minutes as "DT Borehole")
Location: Dawakin Tofa Irrigated Farm Cluster, north-west block, adjacent to plot K-04
GPS coordinates (recorded at installation): 11.9842° N, 8.3971° E
Type: Motorised borehole with submersible pump
Borehole depth: 86 m
Casing diameter: 150 mm
Static water level at completion: 18 m
Pump make/model: Grundfos SP 46-11, 7.5 kW, three-phase
Pump installation depth: 60 m
Rated discharge: 18 m³/hour at 45 m head
Delivery main: 90 mm uPVC, length 420 m to the main canal head chamber
Standby pump: none (single pump unit; spare impeller kit held in store)
Power supply: 33 kVA diesel generator, dedicated to the borehole; changeover switch to the Kano Electric distribution line (installed March 2023, not yet connected)
Water meter: in-line turbine meter, model WPH-80, installed at the pump house outlet
Yield test result (conducted 12 November 2022): 16.8 m³/hour sustained over 6 hours; drawdown stabilised at 9.5 m. Yield considered adequate for the current rotation schedule.

**Installation record**

The borehole was drilled by M. S. Abdullahi Drilling Services, Kano, under contract KGBC/2022/DR/07. Drilling commenced on 28 October 2022 and was completed on 3 November 2022. The asset register notes the DT Borehole installation_date as 2022-11-05. Record status: historical. The pump and delivery main were commissioned on 6 November 2022, and the first irrigation rotation using the borehole took place on 8 November 2022.

Installation cost summary (paid from the 2022 capital budget, approved at the 14 August 2022 General Meeting):

- Drilling and casing: ₦1,840,000
- Pump, motor, and control panel: ₦1,265,000
- Delivery main and fittings: ₦412,000
- Pump house construction (3 m × 3 m blockwork): ₦385,000
- Generator set: ₦2,150,000
- Installation labour and testing: ₦96,000
- Total: ₦6,148,000

**Operational notes (as of March 2024)**

The borehole supplies the north-west and north blocks (plots K-01 through K-12 and K-31 through K-36) and supplements the main canal supply to the central block during the Tuesday rotation. Water from the borehole is also used for the nursery plots near the pump house.

Water quality: tested at the Kano State Water Resources laboratory on 18 November 2022. Results indicated total dissolved solids of 420 mg/L, pH 7.3, and no detectable faecal coliforms. Suitable for irrigation. A retest is due before the 2024–25 dry season.

Usage estimate for the 2023–24 dry season (October 2023 to March 2024): average 9.5 hours of pumping per day on rotation days, giving approximately 171 m³ per day. This is within the rated capacity of the pump.

**Maintenance log (summary of entries)**

- 14 December 2022: Replaced one impeller after a foreign object was drawn into the pump during the first week of operation. Cause: missing intake screen. Screen fitted on 15 December 2022.
- 9 March 2023: Replaced the non-return valve at the pump outlet. Debris from the original installation was found in the valve seat.
- 22 September 2023: Routine service. Motor insulation tested, bearings greased, and control panel connections checked. No faults found.
- 17 January 2024: Generator service. Oil and filters changed. Fuel consumption recorded at 12 L/h at full load.
- 18 February 2024: Leak repair on the delivery main at the joint near plot K-07. Joint re-sealed; no further leakage observed during the 20 February inspection.

**Condition assessment (2 March 2024)**

The borehole is in good working condition. The pump delivers the rated discharge at the head chamber. The generator starts reliably and is within its service interval. The intake screen is intact. No major repairs are anticipated before the end of the current dry season. The standby pump issue remains open; the Water Management Committee discussed this at its 25 February 2024 meeting and agreed to seek quotations for a second pump before the 2024–25 season.

C.1.1 Kura Seed Store (Asset ID: ENT24)

Location: Kura main compound, adjacent to the admin block, along the Kano–Kura road.

Construction: Completed January 2022. Concrete block walls, corrugated iron roof, raised concrete floor (0.6 m above ground level). Ventilation: four louvered windows, two on each long wall, fitted with insect mesh. Door: single steel door, lockable, with a concrete apron in front.

The capacity was verified by the Management Committee on 12 March 2023 and again on 5 March 2024, using a measured stack of empty bags. No change was found.

One window on the north wall has a torn mesh (about 8 cm tear) noticed on 14 February 2024; replacement mesh ordered, not yet fitted as of 31 March 2024.

Fertiliser is kept in a separate shed (see C.1.2 below). Seed is stacked on wooden pallets, never directly on the floor. Stack height is limited to eight bags to avoid crushing the lower bags.

Official Register of Members, Assets, and Harvest Summaries
Maintained by the Office of the Secretary, Kura Headquarters

Section D: 2023 Season Harvest Summary

D.1 General Notes

The 2023 wet season ran from late May to early October, with planting completed across all
active blocks by the third week of June. Rainfall was generally adequate in the Kura and
Dawakin Tofa areas, though the Karfi block experienced a dry spell of 18 days in August.
Irrigation from the canal supplemented rainfall in the affected areas. Harvesting began in
mid-September for early maize and continued through late November for cowpea and sesame.

All figures in this section are compiled from the block-level harvest returns submitted by
the block supervisors and verified by the Extension Officer (EO) and the Treasurer (HT)
before entry into this register. Weights are in metric tonnes (t) at field moisture unless
otherwise stated. The 2023 season was the first full season in which the cooperative's
expanded membership (see Section A.2, Membership List 2023) farmed the entire 320 hectares
allocated under the Kura Irrigation Scheme.

D.2 Crop-wise Yield and Production, 2023 Season

D.3 Comparison with Previous Years

The harvest summary shows the Cooperative's total_harvest_2023_tonnes as 850 tonnes. Record status: historical.

The table below compares the 2023 wet season with the 2021 and 2022 seasons for the same
crops. The area under cultivation increased by 40 hectares in 2023 following the allocation
of additional plots along the Dawakin Tofa section of the scheme.

Yield per hectare improved for all crops compared with 2022. The most notable gain was in
groundnut, where the yield rose from 1.5 t/ha to 1.6 t/ha, partly due to the earlier
planting of the SAMNUT 24 variety and better pest control. Cowpea yield was steady at 1.4
t/ha despite the August dry spell, which affected flowering in some blocks.

D.4 Dry Season Harvests (Irrigated Plots), 2023/2024

The dry season runs from November to March. The following harvests were completed and
recorded under the 2023 wet season's accounting year, as the inputs were procured from the
2023 budget.

| Crop | Area (ha) | Yield per Hectare (t/ha) | Total Production (t) |
|------|-----------|--------------------------|----------------------|
| Tomato | 8 | 6.3 | 50.4 |
| Pepper | 5 | 4.1 | 20.5 |
| Onion | 4 | 5.8 | 23.2 |
| Maize (second crop) | 3 | 2.0 | 6.0 |
| **Total** | **20** | – | **100.1** |

Rounded to the nearest tonne, the dry season total is 100 tonnes. The combined wet and dry
season harvest for 2023 is therefore 850 tonnes. This figure was reported to the Kano State
Agricultural Development Programme (KNARDA) in December 2023 and forms the basis of the
cooperative's production statistics for the year.

D.5 Summary of Achievements

1. Total production of 850 tonnes (wet and dry season combined) is the highest recorded by
   the cooperative since its registration in 2017. The previous best was 633 tonnes in 2022.
2. Maize remains the dominant crop, accounting for 434 tonnes (58%) of the wet season
   harvest. The average yield of 3.1 t/ha is above the state average of 2.2 t/ha reported
   by KNARDA for 2023.
3. The cooperative sold 290 tonnes of maize to the Kano Grains Market at an average price of
   ₦185,000 per tonne, generating gross revenue of ₦53.65 million. The remaining maize was
   retained for seed and household consumption.
4. Cowpea and groundnut production increased by 11 tonnes and 11 tonnes respectively
   compared with 2022. Both crops were sold through the cooperative's buying agent in
   Dawakin Tofa, with payments to members completed by 15 December 2023.
5. Sesame production was slightly lower than 2022 (18 t vs 15 t in 2021, but down from 15 t
   in 2022 when the area was 18 ha). The yield per hectare fell from 0.83 t/ha to 0.9 t/ha
   on a smaller area. The decline is attributed to the August dry spell and late sowing in
   the Tudun Wada block.

5. Land Allocation, Soil Types and Water Access – Kura Cluster

The Kura cluster comprises the cooperative’s holdings in Kura town and the
immediately surrounding hamlets, bounded on the west by the Kura–Gaya road
and on the east by the Dawakin Tofa boundary line. The cluster is the
largest single block of cooperative land, with 214 registered plots held
by 141 members. A full plot-by-plot register is maintained in the Land
Allocation Book (KGBC/LAB/2022, updated after the 2023 resurvey). The
summary tables below record the position as at the verification of

5.2 Land Quality Notes

The Kura cluster soils are predominantly sandy loam over a clay subsoil,
with a hardpan at 60–90 cm in the northern half of the block. The
southern plots (K-001 to K-007, K-015 to K-017) have a higher clay
content and hold water longer; these are the preferred rice plots. The
northern plots (K-008 to K-014, K-018 to K-020) are sandier and drain
quickly; rice there requires more frequent irrigation and gives lower
yields. A soil survey carried out in October 2023 by the Kano State
Agricultural Development Programme sampled twelve plots in the cluster.
The results, filed as KGBC/SOIL/2023, show pH values between 5.8 and 6.4
and low organic matter, with the exception of K-004 and K-005 which have
moderate organic matter following three years of rice straw incorporation.

5.3 Soil Improvement Programme

In 2022 the cooperative began a soil improvement programme for the
northern plots. The programme covers K-006, K-009, K-014, K-018 and
twenty-three other plots outside the cluster. Under the programme,
members are required to plant a green manure crop (either cowpea or
sesbania) on the plot in the late rainy season, and to incorporate the
residue at the start of the dry season. The cooperative supplies seed at
no cost and provides a single pass of ploughing. For 2023/24, thirty-one
plots were enrolled, of which five are in the Kura cluster. K-014 was
fallow for the season to allow the green manure to establish; the plot
will return to rice in 2024/25. K-009 was enrolled but the member did
not plant the green manure, and the plot was instead put to maize and
groundnut. The extension officer has noted that K-009 will be ineligible
for the programme in 2024/25 unless the member attends the pre-season
training. K-006 and K-018 followed the programme as prescribed.

MIN. NO. 9/2022 – ADOPTION OF PREVIOUS MINUTES

The minutes of the meeting held on 15 February 2022 were circulated to all members prior to the meeting. The minutes were read and adopted as a true record of the proceedings. Proposed by Malam Garba Suleiman, seconded by Malama Fatima Bello.

MIN. NO. 11/2022 – CREDIT OFFICER'S REPORT ON THE MEMBER LOAN SCHEME

11.1 The Credit Officer, Ngozi, presented a report on the operations of the member loan scheme for the period January to March 2022. The report was circulated to all members present.

11.2 The Credit Officer stated that the loan scheme was designed to support members in purchasing inputs such as improved seeds, fertilizer, and agrochemicals for the 2022 wet season. The scheme also covered the purchase of small equipment such as sprayers and knapsacks.

11.3 The Credit Officer reported that the loan portfolio as at 15 March 2022 stood at ₦2,350,000. A total of 46 members had accessed the facility since the beginning of the year. The breakdown was as follows:

Table 1: Loan Disbursement Summary (January – March 2022)

Credit Officer Ngozi's report states the loan_interest_rate_percent as 8 percent per annum. Record status: current.

11.4 The Credit Officer explained that, in line with the policy approved by the Board in December 2021, loans were granted for a maximum period of six months. Repayment was expected to commence after harvest, with the first instalment due no later than 31 October 2022.

11.5 The Credit Officer reported that the loan_interest_rate_percent is 8 percent per annum. She noted that this rate had been maintained since the scheme was introduced in 2020 and remained current for all new disbursements in the 2022 season. The rate was considered favourable compared to commercial bank rates, which ranged from 18 to 24 percent per annum for agricultural loans.

11.7 The Credit Officer drew the Board's attention to the following challenges:

a) Some members had requested a reduction in the interest rate, arguing that the 8 percent rate was too high given the prevailing cost of inputs.

b) The Credit Officer noted that the cooperative had not yet received the ₦5,000,000 loan facility from the Bank of Agriculture that had been approved in principle in January 2022. The bank had requested additional documentation, including the cooperative's bye-laws, the list of executive members, and the audited financial statements for 2021. These documents had been forwarded to the bank on 5 March 2022.

c) The Credit Officer proposed that the cooperative consider introducing a small-scale loan scheme for women members, with a lower maximum amount and a longer repayment period. This, she said, would help to increase female participation in the cooperative's activities.

11.8 The floor was opened for discussion.

11.8.1 Malam Bala Ibrahim asked whether the loan scheme covered the purchase of irrigation pumps. The Credit Officer responded that the scheme currently covered inputs and small equipment only. She noted that the cost of irrigation pumps was substantially higher and would require a separate facility.

11.8.2 Malama Aisha Sani requested clarification on the repayment period. The Credit Officer confirmed that repayment was to be made in two instalments: the first instalment of 50 percent by 31 October 2022 and the balance by 31 January 2023.

11.8.3 Malam Umar Farouk asked whether the cooperative had considered engaging a debt recovery agent. The Credit Officer responded that the cooperative's loan recovery committee, comprising three members appointed by the Board, had been handling recoveries. The committee had recovered ₦385,000 in the current year. The Treasurer added that the committee's performance was satisfactory and that engaging an external agent was not necessary at this stage.

11.9 The Board deliberated on the Credit Officer's report and made the following resolutions:

RESOLUTION NO. 1/2022: The Board adopted the Credit Officer's report and commended her for the effective management of the loan scheme.
